# Leachate plume delineation and monitoring-well design for Zelena Petlja's storage yard

## Verified facts
- The company reports leachate from its temporary storage yard has started seeping toward the site boundary, and its sampling returned COD of 3,400 mg/L, well above the threshold triggering a formal response. [F1]
- The inspectorate ordered four groundwater monitoring wells within 120 days and a remediation proposal, with the 120-day deadline running out in late June 2024. [F2]
- Only a 1993 hydrogeological sketch exists; neither contamination extent nor seasonal groundwater flow direction is known. [F3]
- The requested output is a leachate containment and treatment proposal acceptable to the inspectorate, not only monitoring. [F4]
- The company states it has no dedicated research budget or laboratory beyond the basic wet-chemistry bench used for leachate monitoring. [F5]
- The researcher's industry experience includes advising on site characterisation methodology and monitoring network design. [F6]
- His open_to record lists joint projects with companies working on water supply, environmental monitoring, or geospatial data services, and contract research on site-specific hydrogeological assessment or recharge studies. [F7]
- His published work used a network of 18 multi-level piezometers installed at three transects perpendicular to the riverbank. [F8]

## Our inference
- This suggests his monitoring-network experience can be adapted, but his documented sites are bank-filtration, recharge and canal settings, not waste-yard leachate; the transfer should be tested first.
- Because the evidence is particle-tracking travel times rather than reactive transport, predicting COD attenuation is likely unproven here and should be treated as a hypothesis.
- With only a 1993 sketch and unknown seasonal flow, siting wells before reconnaissance risks off-plume wells; the project is conditional until availability is confirmed.

## Proposed next steps
- First experiment (proposed, 30 days): a reconnaissance campaign before final well siting, testing whether lowland alluvial monitoring methods transfer to a waste-yard leachate setting. Baseline: the 1993 sketch and the company's 3,400 mg/L COD result. The researcher designs temporary piezometer/water-level and boundary-sampling points; the company provides site access, existing data and in-house COD measurements. Measure hydraulic heads, depth to water and COD at the yard boundary and suspected flow paths, repeated after 3–4 weeks. Go/no-go: proceed to final four-well design only if a coherent head gradient and elevated-COD signal appear along at least two transects; otherwise revise the conceptual model and brief the inspectorate before drilling. Proposed targets: reconnaissance report by day 30, four wells by day 90, containment/treatment proposal by late June 2024; final-submission go/no-go: submit only after pre-submission review confirms the order's required elements are addressed; acceptance is a negotiation target, not a promise.
- Final four-well design and installation: researcher specifies screen depths, siting and sampling/head schedule; company handles drilling procurement, permits and contractor access. Proposed check: four wells completed and surveyed by day 90, with confirmatory samples sent to an accredited laboratory if required.
- Containment and treatment proposal: researcher and company prepare options from monitoring results and hold a pre-submission meeting with the inspectorate. Proposed criterion: written confirmation that the submission addresses the order's required elements before the late-June deadline.
- After first sampling round, produce a concise conceptual site model and data package for management; decide whether to continue monitoring, add wells, or proceed to a treatment pilot. Proposed target: draft package within 10 working days of sample results.

## Open questions
- Is the researcher available to start field work within the 120-day spring 2024 window, given availability is recorded as unknown?
- Who will carry out and fund drilling and installation of the four wells, and which permits are required?
- What site information exists beyond the 1993 sketch: depth to water table, liner construction, existing boreholes, nearby production or monitoring wells?
- Which parameters and analytical standards will the Subotica Environmental Inspectorate require, and is an accredited laboratory available for confirmatory analyses?
- What waste types and volumes were stored in the yard over twelve years, and were any hazardous items present that would change leachate composition?

Her manganese/iron work likely transfers conceptually, but published manganese coagulation evidence is synthetic water with higher Mn and alum/KMnO4, not PACl/ferric laundry greywater, so transfer must be tested.

proposedActions: Proposed first experiment: at one affected laundry site, sample raw greywater, post-coagulation, post-filter and holding-tank outlet daily for four weeks, plus filter-media and tank-sediment cores. Baseline: current PACl/ferric operation. Proposed company contribution: process flow, site access and on-site kit readings; proposed researcher contribution: ICP-OES and voltammetric/spectrophotometric manganese speciation plus jar tests on real greywater. Run stage-isolated tests changing one factor per series: current versus prior dose/pH, filtered versus unfiltered, and tank-sediment contact. Measure dissolved, colloidal and particulate Mn, Fe, turbidity, pH and ORP. Go/no-go by month 3: identify one stage where Mn rises above the 0.04-0.07 mg/L raw range and a candidate adjustment keeping outlet Mn <=0.10 mg/L and Fe <=0.30 mg/L in bench/pilot tests without major equipment replacement; otherwise expand diagnosis.

Proposed timeline: weeks 1-2 sampling plan; weeks 3-8 stage sampling and speciation; weeks 9-14 jar/column tests isolating coagulation, filter media and tank cycling; weeks 15-16 report and options, targeting month 4 before the five-month reinspection.

Proposed success criteria, as targets not guarantees: one site verifies outlet Mn <=0.10 mg/L and Fe <=0.30 mg/L over two weeks under existing operation after one stage-specific change; two independent sample sets link the increase to a named stage; the change uses existing equipment; reinspection package ready before deadline.

Proposed second phase if filter media or tank cycling is implicated: column tests with current media and tank sediment under real greywater, one factor per run, Faculty lab analysis and company field support; stop if no stage-specific cause or major equipment replacement is required.
questions: Can AquaCikl provide a process flow diagram with all sampling points, confirm stage-wise access at the three installations, and supply filter-media and holding-tank cleaning/backwash history plus any prior media/tank analyses?
What client-process chemicals enter the raw greywater, and could upstream laundry or food operations release manganese or manganese-complexing agents?
Can the Faculty of Technology laboratory perform ICP-OES and speciation under the university service agreement, and what sample volumes, preservation and turnaround would AquaCikl need?
Prof. Žigić's availability is unknown; can she confirm availability to start a joint project within five months, and what budget, data-sharing, IP and publication terms would both sides propose?
Will results need confirmation by the accredited external laboratory in Zrenjanin for reinspection, and what reporting format does the regulator require?
content.markdown:
# Locating and controlling manganese release in AquaCikl greywater recycling

## Verified facts
- AquaCikl's analysers read 0.18 mg/L manganese at the coagulation outlet across three client sites; SR-IED-2023 limits are 0.10 mg/L manganese and 0.30 mg/L iron. [F1]
- One large laundry client faces reinspection in five months. [F2]
- Raw greywater entering the plant contains 0.04-0.07 mg/L manganese, and the company can pull samples at every process stage with its on-site kit. [F3]
- Increasing coagulant dose by 30% and dropping pH from 7.4 to 6.9 during coagulation gave no meaningful improvement. [F4]
- The company's acceptable outcome is a root-cause finding and a specific process change implementable at existing installations without replacing major equipment. [F5]
- The company can dedicate two senior process engineers, one lab technician, up to four months, and access to three operating installations. [F6]
- Prof. Žigić's group focuses on transition-metal speciation, including iron and manganese, and redox transformations in aqueous systems. [F7]
- Prof. Žigić prefers collaborations where the Faculty of Technology laboratory performs analytical work rather than acting solely as a subcontractor. [F8]

## Our inference
- The raw-to-outlet gap and failed dose/pH trials suggest manganese is released or held in filters/tanks, so coagulation-only optimisation likely misses the source; stage-wise speciation is needed.
- Her manganese/iron work likely transfers conceptually, but published manganese coagulation evidence is synthetic water with higher Mn and alum/KMnO4, not PACl/ferric laundry greywater, so transfer must be tested.
- Her laboratory capability fits a joint project, but availability is unknown, making timing conditional against the five-month deadline.

## Proposed next steps
- Proposed first experiment: at one affected laundry site, sample raw greywater, post-coagulation, post-filter and holding-tank outlet daily for four weeks, plus filter-media and tank-sediment cores. Baseline: current PACl/ferric operation. Proposed company contribution: process flow, site access and on-site kit readings; proposed researcher contribution: ICP-OES and voltammetric/spectrophotometric manganese speciation plus jar tests on real greywater. Run stage-isolated tests changing one factor per series: current versus prior dose/pH, filtered versus unfiltered, and tank-sediment contact. Measure dissolved, colloidal and particulate Mn, Fe, turbidity, pH and ORP. Go/no-go by month 3: identify one stage where Mn rises above the 0.04-0.07 mg/L raw range and a candidate adjustment keeping outlet Mn <=0.10 mg/L and Fe <=0.30 mg/L in bench/pilot tests without major equipment replacement; otherwise expand diagnosis.
- Proposed timeline: weeks 1-2 sampling plan; weeks 3-8 stage sampling and speciation; weeks 9-14 jar/column tests isolating coagulation, filter media and tank cycling; weeks 15-16 report and options, targeting month 4 before the five-month reinspection.
- Proposed success criteria, as targets not guarantees: one site verifies outlet Mn <=0.10 mg/L and Fe <=0.30 mg/L over two weeks under existing operation after one stage-specific change; two independent sample sets link the increase to a named stage; the change uses existing equipment; reinspection package ready before deadline.
- Proposed second phase if filter media or tank cycling is implicated: column tests with current media and tank sediment under real greywater, one factor per run, Faculty lab analysis and company field support; stop if no stage-specific cause or major equipment replacement is required.

## Open questions
- Can AquaCikl provide a process flow diagram with all sampling points, confirm stage-wise access at the three installations, and supply filter-media and holding-tank cleaning/backwash history plus any prior media/tank analyses?
- What client-process chemicals enter the raw greywater, and could upstream laundry or food operations release manganese or manganese-complexing agents?
- Can the Faculty of Technology laboratory perform ICP-OES and speciation under the university service agreement, and what sample volumes, preservation and turnaround would AquaCikl need?
- Prof. Žigić's availability is unknown; can she confirm availability to start a joint project within five months, and what budget, data-sharing, IP and publication terms would both sides propose?
- Will results need confirmation by the accredited external laboratory in Zrenjanin for reinspection, and what reporting format does the regulator require?

sources.quote: dissertation on Bayesian state-space models for bus travel time estimation using archived AVL data
Segment-level mean absolute error (MAE) is reduced by 18% compared with a historic-average baseline.
Code is provided as open-source Python modules.
Workload is moderate; she can take on one new collaboration in 2026.
She prefers collaborations where her group retains the right to publish anonymised results.

facts.text: Risk from her work: a Novi Sad model fine-tuned on Subotica reached 52 seconds MAE per stop-to-stop segment, but topology differences limited gains beyond about 8 weeks of fine-tuning; conformal prediction held 90% coverage at the cost of wider intervals.

sources.quote: GRU model pre-trained on five years of Novi Sad AVL data can be fine-tuned with limited data (4 weeks) from Subotica
fine-tuned model achieves MAE of 52 seconds per stop-to-stop segment
network topology differences limit gains beyond approximately 8 weeks of fine-tuning data
Conformal prediction maintains nominal 90% coverage most consistently, at the cost of wider intervals.

inferences: Her reported errors are segment-level or 15-minute-ahead, not the end-to-end 90-second/85% contract metric, so the SLA must be measured on company data.
Her filter assumes 30–90-second pings while the company logs every ten seconds; denser data likely changes preprocessing assumptions and needs revalidation.
Lightweight nightly-retrained models likely fit the company's limited Python maintenance capacity better than GPU-heavy models, suggesting state-space or fine-tuned GRU with a retraining runbook.
proposedActions: First experiment (proposed): use 12 months of the 340-bus AVL archive; baselines are today's timetable-plus-offset PassengerView and a historic-average segment model. Re-run her preprocessing on the 10-second stream; compare a revalidated state-space model and a company-fine-tuned GRU. Measure the contract metric—share of displayed stop-level ETAs within 90 seconds—on held-out weeks, stratified by peak, off-peak, roadworks and bad weather, with actual arrival as door-open event plus a stop-line sensitivity check. Proposed go/no-go: at least 85% within 90 seconds overall and no scope stratum below a negotiated floor; otherwise stop. Researcher contributes modelling and evaluation design; company contributes data access, timetable logs and acceptance conditions.

Sign a data-sharing agreement and write a joint evaluation protocol defining actual arrival, scope, disruption strata, and the 90-second/85% computation. Proposed timeline as negotiation target: protocol month 1, experiment months 2–6, serving and handover months 7–12; success criteria are the SLA plus a reproducible retraining and monitoring runbook.

Isolate one suspected drift factor at a time: compare roadworks-only and bad-weather-only cases with and without integrated weather, so results say which factor matters. Test door-open events as a dwell proxy where passenger counters are absent, and report where load-aware gains do not transfer.

Plan serving and handover: expose the Python model behind a REST service consumed by the Java/Spring PassengerView path and GTFS-Realtime output on the Kubernetes cluster, with nightly retraining on a standard server and a data-engineer runbook.
questions: What exactly counts as actual arrival for the 90-second/85% SLA—door-open event, stop-line crossing or another signal—and which lines, periods and disruption conditions are in scope?
Will the full historical AVL archive and timetable logs be available under a signed data-sharing agreement, and what known data-quality issues exist in the 2.8-billion-row table?
Can weather data be integrated, or should the first model be weather-blind; and are passenger counters available, or only door-open events and odometer?
The researcher's availability is not confirmed: can she confirm capacity and effort from 2026, and can the company accept her preference to publish anonymised results?

How will the Python model be served and owned inside the Java/Spring Kubernetes stack after the project, and are Q3 2024 go-live, the 12-month window, and any budget or compute allocation still operative?

content.markdown:
# Hybrid Recommender Prototype for Small E-Commerce Catalogues

## Verified facts
- The company's material states that with only 500–2,000 transactions per client its collaborative filtering models gave worse results than simple best-seller sorting, with the largest dataset at 1,900 completed orders over eighteen months and the smallest around 520, and that it cannot wait for larger datasets; it also reports the purchase co-occurrence matrix was too sparse to be useful. [F1]
- The company's material reports that simple best-seller sorting outperformed the model in its one client A/B test and that a working prototype for one client would be enough to start. [F2]
- The company can give full read access to anonymised transaction and product catalogue data under a data-sharing agreement. [F3]
- The company can allocate one mid-level developer for roughly one day per week and reports it has not done a structured collaboration with a university or research institution, while Erić is cautious about commitments requiring more than one day per week outside the faculty during the academic semester. [F4]
- The client stack includes PHP/Laravel backend development, MySQL/MariaDB transactional data, and WooCommerce with custom REST API integrations. [F5]
- Erić lists joint projects with retail technology companies as open; her dissertation concerned hybrid recommendation strategies for data-sparse retail environments, and her group combines content-based filtering with behavioural signals from sparse transaction logs typical of small and medium retail businesses. [F6]
- Erić's work shows structured product attribute data can be encoded into feature vectors for new-item recommendation, but it notes limitations in attribute completeness and supplier data availability, and warns that content-based methods tend to over-specialise recommendations. [F7]
- Erić's matrix-factorization study found hit rate drops below the non-personalised popularity baseline at 0.3% density. [F8]

## Our inference
- Because Erić's evaluations use grocery, clothing, pharmacy and home-goods retail data rather than Harmat's e-commerce catalogues, transfer to a Harmat client is plausible but unproven; the first test should therefore be a one-client transfer check.
- A content-heavy hybrid is more likely to beat best-seller sorting on small catalogues if metadata is rich enough, but sparse co-occurrence and over-specialisation could erase the gain, so a one-factor-at-a-time comparison should show which signal matters.
- The proposal is conditional because Erić's availability is unknown and semester-limited; joint-project willingness is open, but a one-day-per-week cadence still needs her confirmation.

## Proposed next steps
- First experiment: select one Harmat client after a data-sharing agreement and use its anonymised completed orders, expected in the 500–2,000 range, plus product catalogue metadata, split by time into train/test; baseline is best-seller sorting. Build two variants: content-only attribute similarity and a content plus session/co-occurrence hybrid. Measure offline precision@5 and recall@5 against the baseline, then, if offline results justify it, run a small A/B test on product pages against best-seller. Researcher contribution: Erić designs and evaluates the recommender; company contribution: Harmat supplies data access and one developer for Laravel/MySQL/WooCommerce integration and logging. This tests transfer from Erić's published retail settings to one Harmat catalogue. Go/no-go: proceed only if the hybrid beats best-seller by an agreed relative margin (proposed ≥10% on precision@5) and metadata completeness passes an agreed threshold; stop if metadata is too incomplete or no variant beats popularity. Proposed timeline: 4 weeks data audit and offline test, 4–6 weeks integration/A/B if go.
- Agree before start the A/B success criterion: metric (click-through or add-to-cart rate), minimum relative lift over best-seller, evaluation window and minimum traffic; treat these as negotiation targets, not guarantees, and confirm the one-client test has enough traffic for reliability.
- Audit product metadata per client: descriptions, categories, attributes, price tier, supplier and languages; quantify completeness and flag fields needed for attribute vectors and explanations.
- Run a one-factor-at-a-time comparison (best-seller, content-only, content+session, content+co-occurrence) on the same temporal split to identify which factor drives any gain, and document integration constraints for Laravel/MySQL/WooCommerce.

## Open questions
- Which client and catalogue will be used for the prototype, and what are the exact transaction, user, SKU and time-span counts?
- What product metadata fields are available (descriptions, categories, attributes, price tier, supplier), in which languages, and how complete are they?
- What is the precise success criterion versus best-seller sorting: metric, minimum lift, evaluation window and available A/B traffic?
- Can Harmat confirm the joint-project format, data-sharing agreement, anonymisation procedure and data access mechanism, and name who will do the PHP/Vue/MySQL/WooCommerce integration?
- Can Branislava Erić confirm availability for the required one-day-per-week cadence during semester and summer flexibility, and is there interest in an industrial PhD track, which is currently unknown?
